questions.scenario: The core principle of Segregation of Duties is:
options: Senior people need no controls
No single person may hold two of: authorize, execute, record — for the same flow
Everyone must work in separate buildings
Only finance staff may touch any screen
questions.explanation: Splitting the three duties means fraud requires collusion (risky, traceable) instead of one quiet decision. It protects honest staff from temptation and suspicion alike.
wrongExplanations: Seniority raises risk exposure — MD-level fraud is the most expensive kind.
Physical separation is one tactic; DUTY separation is the principle.
Operational staff legitimately execute their own flows — with checks around them.

questions.scenario: Which role pair is TOXIC (must never combine in one person)?
options: Create/modify vendor master + approve payments to vendors
Sales manager + commercial officer
Knitting operator + dyeing operator
HR officer + compliance officer
questions.explanation: That combination enables ghost vendors and bank-account-swap fraud end-to-end. The module's fake-bank-change story died exactly because these duties were split.
wrongExplanations: Different departments sharing context is normal.
Production roles are execution-only within their flows.
Both administrative, neither holds payment keys.

options: Whoever makes fastest checks themselves
Changes/sensitive actions stay PENDING until a DIFFERENT authorized person reviews and approves
Two people type the same entry to compare speed
Makers are junior, checkers are senior, always
questions.explanation: Independent second eyes on every sensitive object — especially master data like vendor bank accounts. Seniority isn't the point; INDEPENDENCE is.
wrongExplanations: Self-checking is the exact failure mode being prevented.
It's a review workflow, not a typing race.
Deputies at any level can check if independent of the maker.

questions.scenario: Why are journal entries corrected by REVERSALS rather than edits or deletes?
options: Reversals look more professional on screens
Immutable history preserves the audit trail: everyone sees what happened AND how it was fixed, tied to approvals
Databases can't update rows
Edits are slower than new entries
questions.explanation: Editable ledgers are unreliable ledgers — auditors treat edit-capable books as compromised evidence. Reversal pairs keep truth complete: mistake visible, correction visible, both approved.
wrongExplanations: Cosmetics never justify control design.
Any database updates rows fine — this is an ACCOUNTING choice.
Speed is irrelevant against integrity.

options: Preventive: SoD, approval limits. Detective: reconciliations, exception reports, cycle counts
Preventive: audits after year-end. Detective: nothing until police arrive
Preventive: hoping. Detective: crying
They're synonyms
questions.explanation: Prevention stops bad entries entering (Module 4's sequence checks too); detection finds what slipped through fast enough to matter. Layers assume each other's failure.
wrongExplanations: Year-end discovery is detective-at-its-worst-delayed; prevention happens BEFORE transactions complete.
Every serious control framework combines both families.
Distinct families with distinct jobs.

questions.scenario: An attacker emails a fake 'vendor bank account change' request. Which control layer does NOT help here?
options: Maker-checker pending state on master changes
Out-of-band callback to the OLD known number
Exception reporting of rejected changes
Increasing the payment approval limit so fewer people review payments
questions.explanation: Raising limits REDUCES review — exactly backwards for fraud resistance. The other three form the layered defense that caught the module's simulated attack.
wrongExplanations: Pending-until-checked blocks solo account swaps.
Callback verification kills spoofed-email attacks dead.
Pattern visibility across attempts exposes campaigns targeting multiple units.

questions.scenario: An executive gets temporary checker rights 'just for today' while the regular checker is on leave. Risk analysis:
options: Safe — it's only one day
Dangerous: dual-role windows are when attackers strike (they watch calendars); proper design uses pre-designated deputies or logged time-boxed elevation
Fine if he promises carefully
Safer than waiting a day for payments
questions.explanation: Segregation exceptions are the attack surface. Emergency access must itself be controlled: pre-approved deputies, time-limited grants, full logging, post-review — never casual sharing.
wrongExplanations: Fraud needs minutes, not days.
Promises aren't controls — Module 12 exists because promises fail.
One day of dual keys can empty years of discipline.

questions.scenario: Which report BEST serves as daily detective control over payables?
options: Employee birthday list
Subledger-vs-GL reconciliation + unmatched-invoice report + rejected-change log reviewed by finance
Annual marketing summary
Buyer satisfaction survey
questions.explanation: Detective controls surface anomalies FAST: layer mismatches (Mod 3), documents missing matches (this module), suspicious activity patterns. Daily cadence keeps investigations trivial.
wrongExplanations: Lovely, irrelevant.
Exactly the trio that catches drift, mismatches, and attacks.
Important commercially; not a payable-integrity control.

questions.scenario: Jamal wants the system to let him approve his own GRNs 'because I'm careful.' Best response:
options: Grant it — careful people need no controls
Refuse kindly: self-approval removes the second set of eyes protecting HIM; QC/another storekeeper provides the independent check
Grant it but ask him to be extra careful
Fire anyone requesting controls changes
questions.explanation: SoD protects the honest from accusation and error alike. The system refusing Jamal IS the company defending his reputation — remember the storekeeper's 'best rejection of my career'.
wrongExplanations: Care is not a control; independence is.
Intentions don't verify quantities — checkers do.
Control requests deserve discussion, not punishment — education first.

questions.scenario: External auditors request evidence that approval limits were enforced all year. Your ERP should answer with:
options: Verbal assurance from the MD
System-generated reports: role/limit configuration history plus sampled transaction trails showing document→approver→entry chains within limits
A promise email from IT
Screenshot of one random payment
questions.explanation: Audit evidence must be systematic and replayable: config-as-was + per-transaction lineage. This is why Modules 0-4 insisted on document references, rule versions, and immutable logs — audit-readiness was designed in from day one.
wrongExplanations: Assurances aren't evidence — auditors test systems, not vibes.
Emails attest intent, not enforcement history.
One screenshot proves one moment, not a year of enforcement.
